shortQuestions: The electrostatic repulsion between protons increases rapidly with Z (it acts between every pair of protons), while the strong nuclear force is short-ranged and acts only between neighbours.
Extra neutrons add attractive strong force without adding repulsion, holding the nucleus together. So heavy nuclei need more neutrons than protons (N/Z ≈ 1.5 for heavy nuclei).
Radium is continuously produced in the uranium-238 decay series.

²³⁸U has a half-life of about 4.5 × 10⁹ years, so it is still plentiful, and its decay chain keeps forming new radium. So radium is found in uranium ores even though its own half-life is only 1600 years.
No. Radioactive decay is a random (spontaneous) process: we can only state the probability per unit time (the decay constant λ) that a nucleus will decay.
The half-life is a statistical quantity that applies to a large number of nuclei; the moment a particular nucleus decays cannot be predicted.
Neutrons have no charge, so they feel no electrostatic repulsion from the nucleus.
Even slow neutrons can approach and enter a nucleus easily; slow neutrons stay near the nucleus longer and are captured readily, causing nuclear reactions such as fission.
When a nucleus absorbs a neutron it becomes neutron-rich (too many neutrons for its number of protons).
To approach the stability line it must convert a neutron into a proton: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄, which is β⁻ decay. β⁺ decay (p → n) would make it even more neutron-rich.
Stability depends on the binding energy per nucleon, which is maximum (≈ 8.8 MeV) near iron-56.
Very light nuclei have few nucleons, so many nucleons are at the surface and the binding energy per nucleon is low; they can become more stable by fusing.
Very heavy nuclei have large proton–proton repulsion that weakens the binding; they become more stable by α-decay or fission.
Reactor fuel is only slightly enriched (about 3–4% ²³⁵U), while a bomb needs highly enriched material (≈ 90%) assembled very rapidly into a supercritical mass.
In a reactor the chain reaction is kept just critical (k = 1) by control rods and the moderator, and it relies on delayed neutrons, so it changes slowly and can be controlled.
If it overheats, the moderator is lost or expands and the reaction slows. A reactor can overheat or melt down, but it cannot explode like a nuclear bomb.
The binding energy per nucleon of light nuclei increases with mass number (e.g. ²H 1.1 MeV, ⁴He 7.1 MeV).
When light nuclei fuse, the product is more tightly bound: its mass is less than the total mass of the reacting nuclei.
The mass defect Δm is released as energy E = Δmc² (e.g. ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV).
Both nuclei are positively charged, so a very large Coulomb barrier repels them; they must have huge kinetic energies to come within range of the strong force.
This needs temperatures of about 10⁷–10⁸ K, at which matter is a plasma, together with high density and long enough confinement time (Lawson criterion).
No material container can hold such hot plasma; it must be confined by strong magnetic fields (tokamak) or by lasers (inertial confinement), which is technically very difficult.
longQuestions: Natural radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable nuclei of heavy elements (Z > 82), such as uranium, thorium and radium, without any external cause. It was discovered by Becquerel in 1896.
The rate of emission is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination; it is a nuclear property.

Classification (by passing the radiation through a magnetic or electric field): α-rays bend slightly one way — they are positively charged helium nuclei (⁴₂He); β-rays bend strongly the other way — they are fast electrons; γ-rays are undeflected — they are uncharged high-energy electromagnetic photons.
Penetration: α stopped by paper, β by a few mm of aluminium, γ needs several cm of lead. Ionising power is greatest for α and least for γ.
A mass spectrometer separates ions according to their mass and measures their masses (it shows the existence of isotopes).

Construction: an ion source (ions of charge q accelerated by p.d. V), a velocity selector (crossed E and B fields), and a deflection chamber with a uniform magnetic field B, plus a detector/photographic plate.
Velocity selector: only ions with qE = qvB pass straight through, so all have speed v = E/B.
In the deflection chamber the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) and m = qBr/v = qB r B/E.
Ions of different mass (isotopes) travel on circles of different radii and strike the plate at different places; the positions give the masses and the intensities give the relative abundances.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number Z (same number of protons and electrons) but different mass numbers A (different numbers of neutrons).
They have the same chemical properties but different physical (nuclear) properties.
Examples: hydrogen — ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium); carbon — ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C (radioactive); uranium — ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U; chlorine — ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
Isotopes are separated and identified with a mass spectrometer.
Mass defect: the mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons. Δm = Zm_p + (A − Z)m_n − m_nucleus.
Binding energy: the energy equivalent of the mass defect, E_b = Δmc² (1 u = 931.5 MeV); it is the energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons, or released when they combine.
Example: ⁴He: Δm = 0.0304 u, E_b = 28.3 MeV.

Binding energy per nucleon E_b/A measures stability; its graph against A rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near ⁵⁶Fe (≈ 8.8 MeV) and falls slowly for heavy nuclei — explaining why fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy.
Half-life T½ is the time in which half of the radioactive nuclei present in a sample decay.
Decay law: N = N₀e^(−λt). Putting N = N₀/2 at t = T½ gives e^(−λT½) = ½, so T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ.
After n half-lives the remaining number is N₀/2ⁿ (½, ¼, ⅛ …).

Half-life is characteristic of each radioisotope and ranges from fractions of a second to billions of years (e.g. ¹³¹I 8 days, ¹⁴C 5730 years, ²³⁸U 4.5 × 10⁹ years). It is unaffected by physical or chemical conditions.

A nuclear reaction occurs when a nucleus is struck by a particle (proton, neutron, α-particle, deuteron, photon) and changes into a different nucleus, e.g. ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H (Rutherford, 1919).
In every nuclear reaction the total charge (Z) and the total number of nucleons (A) are conserved, as are energy and momentum.
Q-value: Q = (mass of reactants − mass of products)c². If Q > 0, energy is released (exoergic); if Q < 0, energy must be supplied (endoergic).
Examples: neutron capture, transmutation, fission and fusion.
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-sized nuclei when it absorbs a neutron, with release of energy and more neutrons.
Example: ¹n + ²³⁵U → ²³⁶U* → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3¹n + about 200 MeV.
Energy: the products have higher binding energy per nucleon, so mass is lost; the mass defect appears mostly as the kinetic energy of the fragments (heat).

Chain reaction: the 2–3 neutrons released can fission further nuclei. If more than one neutron per fission causes further fission, the reaction grows rapidly (bomb); if exactly one does, it is steady (reactor). A minimum (critical) mass is needed.
Fission was discovered by Hahn and Strassmann (1938); it is used in nuclear power stations and atomic bombs.
A nuclear reactor is a device in which a controlled, self-sustaining fission chain reaction produces heat (used to generate electricity).
Principle: controlled chain reaction with on average one neutron from each fission causing one further fission (k = 1).

Construction: fuel rods (enriched uranium); moderator (water, heavy water or graphite) to slow neutrons; control rods (cadmium or boron) to absorb neutrons; coolant (water or CO₂) to remove heat; thick concrete shielding.
Working: heat from fission is carried by the coolant to a heat exchanger, producing steam that drives turbines and generators. Raising or lowering the control rods adjusts the rate of reaction.
Uses: generating electricity, producing radioisotopes for medicine and industry, research, and propulsion of submarines and ships.
Nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus with release of energy.
Energy release: the product is more tightly bound (higher binding energy per nucleon), so its mass is less than that of the reactants; the mass defect is released as E = Δmc².
Examples: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV; in the Sun the proton–proton chain converts four protons into one ⁴He nucleus releasing about 26.7 MeV.

Fusion needs temperatures of about 10⁷ K or more to overcome the Coulomb repulsion (thermonuclear reactions). It powers the Sun and stars and the hydrogen bomb; controlled fusion for electricity is under research (tokamaks).
A radiation detector is a device that detects and counts nuclear radiation by the ionisation or excitation it produces.

GM counter — principle: radiation ionises the gas in a tube and the ions are multiplied by a strong field. Construction: a metal cylinder (cathode) with a thin central wire (anode) at about 400–1000 V, filled with argon at low pressure plus a quenching gas, and a thin mica window. Working: each particle entering produces a few ions; the electrons accelerate to the wire and cause an avalanche of ionisation, giving a pulse that is counted.

Solid-state detector — principle: radiation creates electron–hole pairs in a semiconductor. Construction: a reverse-biased p–n junction (silicon or germanium) with a wide depletion layer. Working: radiation entering the depletion layer creates electron–hole pairs that are swept to the electrodes, giving a pulse proportional to the energy deposited.
Solid-state detectors are compact, fast and measure energies accurately; GM counters are simple and sensitive but cannot measure energy.
Medical diagnosis (tracers): ¹³¹I to study the thyroid, ⁹⁹ᵐTc for bone, heart and brain scans, ²⁴Na to detect blood-flow blockages; PET scans use positron emitters such as ¹⁸F.
Radiotherapy: ⁶⁰Co γ-rays and other sources destroy cancer cells; ¹³¹I treats thyroid cancer.
Sterilisation of surgical instruments and food preservation by γ-irradiation.

Biological research: ¹⁴C and ³²P tracers follow photosynthesis and the uptake of fertilisers by plants; radiation is used to produce improved crop varieties and to control insect pests (sterile insect technique).
Radiocarbon dating (¹⁴C) finds the age of biological remains.
Elementary particles are classified as hadrons and leptons (plus force carriers).

Hadrons feel the strong force and are made of quarks. Baryons (three quarks, half-integer spin) include protons (uud) and neutrons (udd); mesons (quark–antiquark pairs, integer spin) include pions and kaons.
Leptons do not feel the strong force and have no known internal structure: electron, muon, tau and their three neutrinos (plus antiparticles). They have spin ½.

Quarks are the fundamental constituents of hadrons. There are six flavours: up, down, strange, charm, bottom (beauty) and top (truth), with charges +2/3 e or −1/3 e. They carry colour charge and are never found free (quark confinement); they combine into colour-neutral hadrons.
Together with the force-carrying bosons (photon, gluons, W and Z), these form the Standard Model.
